questions.q: Acetophenone is heated with hydrazine and KOH in ethylene glycol at about 200 °C. The product is:
questions.explain: The Wolff–Kishner reduction turns C=O into CH₂: C₆H₅COCH₃ becomes C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, with N₂ and H₂O given off. The benzene ring attached to the C=O is not touched.

questions.q: In the Wolff–Kishner mechanism, the species left on carbon immediately after N₂ is lost is a:
questions.explain: When N₂ departs, the carbon keeps the bonding pair it shared with nitrogen, so it is a carbanion R₂CH⁻, which the solvent then protonates. Drawing a carbocation here is the common mistake.

questions.q: A ketone also contains an ester group that hot KOH would hydrolyse. To convert its C=O into CH₂ without harming the ester, the better choice is:
questions.explain: Esters are base-sensitive and do not survive the hot, strongly basic Wolff–Kishner conditions (Huang–Minlon is the same basic method). Clemmensen does the same C=O → CH₂ change in acid, so it suits base-sensitive compounds.

questions.q: Which sequence converts benzene into n-propylbenzene without a rearranged product?
options: CH₃CH₂COCl/AlCl₃, then NH₂NH₂, KOH, glycol, heat
CH₃CH₂COCl/AlCl₃, then NH₂NH₂ at room temperature only
questions.explain: Friedel–Crafts acylation gives propiophenone with an unrearranged chain, and Wolff–Kishner reduction turns its C=O into CH₂. Direct alkylation with a primary halide gives rearranged products, and hydrazine alone stops at the hydrazone.
